clue.text: Poet depicted in a university study

blocks.note: taken as written
U is the standard abbreviation for university
a den is a private room for work or study

explanation.surface: A portrait of a poet hangs in a study at a university.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden was an Anglo-American twentieth-century poet, so he is an example of the category.

clue.text: Suspect key servant of being a mass killer

indicators.note: something suspect is dodgy and not to be taken at face value, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the twelve letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A trusted servant comes under suspicion as a mass murderer.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a human killer, but the answer is the Kalashnikov rifle, the AK-47.
explanation.definitionFit: The AK-47 assault rifle is the weapon behind countless deaths worldwide, so it can be called a mass killer.

clue.text: Bends over painfully having strong drink on top of another

definitions.text: having strong drink on top of another

blocks.note: first meaning: folds the body forward in pain or laughter

blocks.clueFragment: having strong drink on top of another
blocks.note: second meaning: orders a double measure of spirits, or one more round on top

explanation.surface: Someone drinking shot after shot ends up bent over in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: A double is a twice-sized measure of spirits; to double up can be read as stacking those drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb describes both a body folding in agony and, read literally, piling one double measure of spirits upon another.

clue.text: French name given to commercial traveller

blocks.note: nom is the French word for name
an ad is a commercial or advertisement

explanation.surface: A French salesman on the road is assigned a name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial traveller' looks like one phrase, a sales rep; split it, and 'commercial' is wordplay while 'traveller' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomad wanders from place to place with no fixed home, so is a kind of traveller.

clue.text: Drug no good when engaging in battle

indicators.note: 'no' says the thing named next is absent, so it is taken out of the word

blocks.note: G is the usual abbreviation for good
warfaring means waging war

explanation.surface: A soldier warns that taking a drug in combat is a bad idea.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the G from the participle for waging war.
explanation.definitionFit: Warfarin is an anticoagulant medicine prescribed to thin the blood, so it is a drug.

clue.text: Collapsed having experienced reversal

blocks.note: first meaning: failed, as a business going bust
second meaning: suffered a setback, as a boxer going down or a patient losing consciousness

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversal' here is a setback in fortune, not a wordplay signal to read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a firm going bankrupt or a person sinking after a downturn, matching both collapse and misfortune.

clue.text: US writer in hospital after breakdown following split

indicators.note: 'after' places the single-letter abbreviation behind the decay word

blocks.note: rot is decay or collapse, as when 'the rot sets in' after a rift
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: An American author ends up in hospital after a breakdown that followed a separation.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Roth was a celebrated American novelist, so he is an instance of a US writer.

clue.text: Creature with limb trouble and unwell inside

indicators.note: 'inside' says the word for sick goes within the word for trouble

blocks.note: an arm is a limb
ado means fuss or trouble
ill means unwell

explanation.surface: An animal with a sore leg is also feeling sick.
explanation.definitionFit: The armadillo is an armoured burrowing mammal of the Americas, so it is a creature.

clue.text: Marine features covered in this lesson

indicators.note: something covered in a lesson is contained within its words, spanning the gap between them

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A geography teacher says coastal landforms are taught in today's class.
explanation.definitionFit: Isles are small islands, features rising out of the sea.

clue.text: Mmmmm … sporting achievement that was hard to surpass

definitions.text: sporting achievement that was hard to surpass

blocks.note: surface reading: a murmur of appreciation
setter's reading: four letters standing for minute, then one standing for mile

explanation.surface: An appreciative hum greets a long-unbeaten athletic record.
explanation.walkthrough: M abbreviates both minute and mile; the answer read as letters describes four of the first followed by one of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Running a mile in under four minutes was long thought impossible until Roger Bannister managed it in 1954.

clue.text: Rogue sees attorney rolling in it …

indicators.note: a rogue behaves unpredictably and out of line, so the letters that follow are disordered

blocks.note: the twelve letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A crook spots a lawyer who is very wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's ellipsis links it to the next clue for the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are idioms for being wealthy and living comfortably without money worries.

clue.text: Voiced concern after order is dismissed

indicators.note: 'Voiced' means spoken, so we want a spelling that matches the sound of the word for worry

blocks.note: to order or decree is to rule
a doubt is a concern; it is said without the B

explanation.surface: Someone raises an objection after a court order is thrown out.
explanation.definitionFit: A possibility that is ruled out has been excluded from consideration, i.e. rejected or set aside.

clue.text: Different offspring almost certain to succeed

blocks.note: odd means unusual or different
a son is a child, an offspring

explanation.surface: A child who stands out from the rest looks set to do well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' belongs to the definition, not a signal to cut a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In betting, an odds-on runner is the strong favourite, very likely to win.

clue.text: Patsy's date of birth?

blocks.note: surface reading: the birthday of someone named Patsy
setter's reading: a patsy is a gullible dupe, who 'wasn't born' a day ago, as the saying goes

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'I wasn't born yesterday' means 'I'm not naive', so a patsy, an easily fooled person, is the one who was.
explanation.definitionFit: A gullible person is said to have been born the day before today, so the day before today is the dupe's birth date.

clue.text: … we see her gallivanting around Lima and other places

indicators.note: gallivanting is roaming about, so the letters are moved around freely
'around' says the rearranged letters surround the abbreviation that follows

blocks.note: letters to rearrange
Lima is L in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: We spot a woman roaming about Peru's capital and beyond.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins it to the previous clue for the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in some other place, so it stands for 'other places' in a sentence like 'look in other places'.

clue.text: Variable pay packet leads to such desires

blocks.note: Y is a standard algebraic unknown
earnings are wages, what a pay packet holds

explanation.surface: Fluctuating wages make people long for more.
explanation.definitionFit: Yearnings are longings or cravings, and 'such' points back to the wish for steadier pay.

clue.text: Legal gag slapped on endlessly glib woman

indicators.note: 'endlessly' removes both ends of the word, keeping only its inner letters

blocks.note: the inner pair of letters of the word
an NDA, a non-disclosure agreement, legally stops someone speaking

explanation.surface: A smooth-talking woman is silenced by a gagging order.
explanation.definitionFit: Linda is a woman's first name; crosswords often define names this loosely.

clue.text: Girl entering fresh pasture finds ancient burial site

indicators.note: something entering goes inside, so the single letter is placed within the phrase for new grazing

blocks.note: fresh means new
G is a dictionary abbreviation for girl
a range is open grazing land

explanation.surface: A girl walking into a new field stumbles on a prehistoric grave.
explanation.walkthrough: Newgrange is a Stone Age passage tomb in County Meath, Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Newgrange is a Neolithic passage grave over 5,000 years old, a famous ancient tomb.

clue.text: Show up abruptly at trade shows

indicators.note: abruptly means cut short, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: to show up a fraud is to expose it

explanation.surface: Someone turns up unannounced at exhibitions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show up' looks like 'arrive', but here it means reveal.
explanation.definitionFit: Expos is short for expositions, large exhibitions where companies display goods.

clue.text: Cause of ludicrous honey wars

indicators.note: ludicrous means absurd or ridiculous, so the letters are made nonsense of and rearranged

blocks.note: letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone asks what started some absurd conflicts over honey.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the motive or explanation behind something, which is what a cause is.

clue.text: Oddly, equal pay was enshrined in these regulations

indicators.note: oddly keeps the letters in odd-numbered places, the first, third and so on

blocks.note: take every other letter starting from the first

explanation.surface: Equal pay for women was written into European legislation.
explanation.definitionFit: EU laws are the regulations of the European Union, and equal pay is indeed enshrined in them.

clue.text: River pilots brief crew from the centre

indicators.note: 'from the centre' says take only the middle letters of each word

blocks.note: the two central letters of the six
the central letter of the five
the two central letters of the four

explanation.surface: Riverboat pilots give their crew instructions from the middle of the boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brief' looks like a cut-short signal but is just one of the source words.
explanation.definitionFit: The Loire is the longest river in France.

clue.text: Surreptitiously deleting note would not be cricket? Actually it would

indicators.note: the clue works backwards: deleting the note from the answer would leave the cricket word, so the note goes inside it

blocks.note: a cricket is an insect
re is a note of the sol-fa scale
surface padding: the setter's aside confirming the backwards reading

explanation.surface: Sneaky cheating isn't cricket, says one voice; another replies that, actually, it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not cricket' means unsporting, but take RE out of IN SECRET and you get INSECT, which a cricket is, hence 'Actually it would'.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in secret means doing it surreptitiously, without others knowing.

clue.text: England has Ireland in a spin; how weird

indicators.note: something in a spin is turned around, so the name for Ireland runs the other way

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for England
Eire is the Irish name for Ireland

explanation.surface: A rugby fan marvels at England running rings around Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Eerie means strange and unsettling, a close synonym of weird.

clue.text: Puzzling message insignias regularly reveal

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: take the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Emblems are found to carry a coded meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: A nina is a crossword term for a message hidden in the grid, named after the cartoonist Al Hirschfeld's habit of hiding his daughter Nina's name in drawings.
explanation.definitionFit: A nina is a hidden word or phrase concealed in a puzzle's grid, a message within a puzzle.

clue.text: Criminal reining in caper scamming royal family member?

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, so the letters are bent into a new order

blocks.note: the fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A crook pulls back on a scheme to con a member of a royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the royal is fictitious: the classic email fraud promising a share of a West African fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: The so-called Nigerian prince is the fake royal in a notorious advance-fee email swindle.

clue.text: Classes by extremely lugubrious commanders

indicators.note: 'extremely' points to the extremities, the first and last letters of the next word

blocks.note: genera are taxonomic classes, plural of genus
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: School classes are run by gloomy teachers.
explanation.definitionFit: Generals are senior army officers who command troops.

clue.text: Chose the final three classic test finishes

indicators.note: finishes are endings, so only the closing letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the closing letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A cricket selector picked the side for the last three Test matches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'final' looks like the selection signal, but it is one of the five words; 'finishes' does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Elect means choose by vote; the setter matches it loosely to the past tense, as in a newly elect committee being the ones chosen.
